title: Quadratic convergence of SOS-density bounds on convex bodies

edition_text.PROOF.md:
# A quadratic proxy and an endpoint kernel for convex-body SOS upper bounds

Theorem and explicit construction, 2026-10-11.

The claim concerns the normalized Lebesgue-measure hierarchy. No novelty claim is made.

## 1. Exact claim

Let K be a compact convex subset of R^n with nonempty interior, n >= 1, and let f be a real polynomial. All integrals below are with respect to n-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Put

    f^(r) = inf { integral_K f(x) q(x) dx :
                 q is a sum of squares, degree(q) <= 2r,
                 integral_K q(x) dx = 1 }.

For every integer r >= 1, the construction below proves

    0 <= f^(r) - min_K f <= C_n G / r^2,

where L = n+2,

    C_n = 4 L^2 (pi/2)^(2L) (1 + 2^(n+2)),

and G is the maximum of a nonnegative quadratic Taylor upper proxy defined below. In particular the constant is finite for each fixed K,f. The estimate asserts an upper rate, not a two-sided Theta rate for every f. For constant f the error is zero. It does not assert this rate for arbitrary reference measures.

## 2. Quadratic proxy

Fix any a in K with f(a) = min_K f. Let

    gamma = 1 + (1/2) max_{x in K} || Hessian f(x) ||_op,
    ell(x) = gradient f(a) dot (x-a),
    g(x) = ell(x) + gamma ||x-a||^2,
    G = max_{x in K} g(x),
    u(x) = g(x)/G.

Because K is convex, the segment a+s(x-a), 0 <= s <= 1, lies in K. Minimality of a and the right derivative at s=0 imply ell(x) >= 0 for all x in K. Taylor's formula with integral remainder on this same segment gives

    0 <= f(x)-f(a) <= ell(x) + (gamma-1)||x-a||^2 <= g(x).

The added 1 in gamma guarantees g(x)>0 for x != a. Nonempty interior ensures K contains such an x, so G>0. Thus u is a degree-at-most-two polynomial with 0<=u<=1 on K, u(a)=0. For 0<=s<=1,

    g(a+s(x-a)) = s ell(x) + s^2 gamma ||x-a||^2 <= s g(x).      (1)

Only the finite Hessian bound and the first-order constrained-minimum condition are used here. The argument also applies to objectives that are C^2 on an open neighborhood of K, since the density is built from the quadratic proxy rather than from f itself.

## 3. Relative sublevel-volume growth

For every t>0 let

    S_t = {x in K : u(x)<=t},       F(t)=vol_n(S_t).

For 0<s<=t, put alpha=s/t. By convexity of K and (1),

    a + alpha(S_t-a) is a subset of S_s.

Lebesgue measure scales by alpha^n, hence

    F(s) >= (s/t)^n F(t),
    F(t) <= (t/s)^n F(s).                                      (2)

These assertions hold also for t>1, when S_t=K. In particular, for 0<s<=1,

    F(s) >= s^n vol_n(K) > 0.                                  (3)

No boundary smoothness, semialgebraicity, local cube structure, or positive solid-angle lower bound is required. The key is the relative upper estimate in (2), not just the absolute lower estimate in (3).

## 4. An explicit polynomial endpoint kernel

For an integer m>=1 set N=2m+1 and define

    A_m(t) = (1 + 2 sum_{k=1}^m T_k(1-2t))/N,

where T_k is the Chebyshev polynomial determined by T_k(cos theta)=cos(k theta). Thus A_m is a real polynomial of degree m and A_m(0)=1.

For 0<t<=1, put v=arcsin(sqrt(t)), so 1-2t=cos(2v), 0<v<=pi/2. The finite geometric-sum identity gives

    A_m(t) = sin(Nv)/(N sin(v)) = sin(N arcsin(sqrt(t)))/(N sqrt(t)).      (4)

The triangle inequality applied to the defining cosine sum gives |A_m(t)|<=1; (4) also gives |A_m(t)|<=1/(N sqrt(t)). Therefore

    |A_m(t)| <= min(1, (N sqrt(t))^(-1)),       0<t<=1.           (5)

Put h=N^(-2). If 0<t<=h, then arcsin(sqrt(t)) <= (pi/2)sqrt(t), hence 0<Nv<=pi/2. On this interval sin z >= 2z/pi, while v>=sqrt(t). Substitution in (4) gives

    A_m(t) >= 2/pi,                          0<=t<=h.           (6)

At t=0, (6) follows from A_m(0)=1. The elementary arcsine inequality used above follows by convexity of arcsin on [0,1], which places its graph below the chord joining (0,0) and (1,pi/2).

## 5. Moment ratio: the logarithm-free step

Let L=n+2 and define Q_m(x)=A_m(u(x))^(2L). This is nonnegative everywhere in R^n and is exactly the square of the polynomial A_m(u(x))^L. From (6),

    integral_K Q_m dx >= (2/pi)^(2L) F(h) > 0.                  (7)

By (5), Q_m<=1 on K and, when u>0, Q_m <= (h/u)^L.
Decompose K into {u<=h} and the pairwise disjoint shells

    E_j={x in K : 2^j h < u(x) <= 2^(j+1) h}, j=0,1,2,... .

Only finitely many shells are nonempty because u<=1. On the core,

    integral_{u<=h} u Q_m dx <= h F(h).

On E_j, use u<=2^(j+1)h, Q_m<=2^(-jL), and (2) to obtain

    integral_{E_j} u Q_m dx
      <= 2^(j+1) h 2^(-jL) F(2^(j+1)h)
      <= h F(h) 2^(n+1) 2^(j(n+1-L)).

Since L=n+2, the geometric sum over j>=0 is 2. Consequently,

    integral_K u Q_m dx <= h F(h) (1+2^(n+2)),

and division by (7) yields

    (integral_K u Q_m dx)/(integral_K Q_m dx)
       <= (pi/2)^(2L)(1+2^(n+2))/(2m+1)^2.                     (8)

The oscillation and zeros of A_m cause no difficulty: the denominator uses its uniformly positive core, and every tail estimate is an absolute-value upper bound. No probability mass is silently discarded outside a simplex or local model.

## 6. Degree, normalization, and all integer orders

For r>=2L choose m=floor(r/(2L))>=1. Since degree(u)<=2,

    degree(A_m(u)^L) <= 2mL <= r,
    degree(Q_m) <= 4mL <= 2r.

Thus

    q_r(x)=Q_m(x)/(integral_K Q_m dx)

is a feasible, single-square SOS density for the exact hierarchy in Section 1. Equations (8) and f-f(a)<=Gu give

    0 <= f^(r)-f(a)
       <= integral_K (f-f(a)) q_r dx
       <= G (pi/2)^(2L)(1+2^(n+2))/(2m+1)^2.

For r>=2L, writing b=r/(2L)>=1 gives 2 floor(b)+1>=b, so

    (2m+1)^(-2) <= 4L^2/r^2.

This proves the stated estimate for r>=2L. For 1<=r<2L use the feasible constant density 1/vol_n(K), whose error is at most G; since C_n/r^2>=1, the same estimate holds. This finishes the proof for every integer r>=1.

## 7. What this does and does not establish

The displayed construction proves the scoped Lebesgue-normalized O_{K,f}(r^-2) statement for all fixed convex bodies. A source still listing a weaker bound does not itself establish novelty. No claim that the proof is new is made.

The result does not establish O(r^-2) for every unspecified reference measure: the change-of-variables volume identity behind (2) is specific here to Lebesgue measure. It does not prove the same rate for the weaker push-forward hierarchy using only polynomials of the original objective f, because our density instead uses the quadratic proxy g. It does imply the analogous rate for that push-forward construction when the objective itself is convex, after normalizing its range and adapting the degree count.

No universal positive lower bound applies for each f, since constants have zero error. This proof supplies no counterexample, no exact asymptotic coefficient, and no sharp dimension dependence.


## 8. Source context

The normalization integral_K q dx=1 is essential. Laurent's 2018 workshop contribution prints an incomplete integral constraint in its equations (3) and (4); this document explicitly supplies the probability-density normalization used in the full papers. This is a mathematical scope repair, not an OCR correction.

Slot and Laurent's Theorem 11 proves O(log^2(r)/r^2) for this same convex-body Lebesgue hierarchy. Their Lemma 20 and Corollary 5 control the tail by a global volume bound, divided by a degree-dependent absolute lower bound for the normalization. In the present proof, the relative bound (2) ties each tail shell to the same F(h) appearing in the denominator, so that this factor cancels before the geometric series is summed. The Taylor upper proxy is already a standard reduction in their Lemma 4; the complete endpoint-kernel and relative-volume argument is proved here without importing a convergence theorem.

References (public primary sources):

1. M. Laurent, joint work with E. de Klerk, “Convergence analysis of Lasserre measure-based approximations for polynomial optimization,” Oberwolfach Report 50/2018, printed pp. 2991-2993, PDF pp. 23-25. https://ems.press/journals/owr/articles/16633
2. L. Slot and M. Laurent, “Improved convergence analysis of Lasserre's measure-based upper bounds for polynomial minimization on compact sets,” arXiv:1905.08142v2, Theorem 11, Lemma 20, Corollary 5, and concluding questions. https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.08142 ; DOI: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10107-020-01468-3
3. L. Slot and M. Laurent, “Near-optimal analysis of Lasserre's univariate measure-based bounds for multivariate polynomial optimization,” arXiv:2001.11289v2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.11289 ; DOI: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10107-020-01586-y
4. M. Laurent and L. Slot, “An Overview of Convergence Rates for Sum of Squares Hierarchies in Polynomial Optimization,” final 2026 chapter, Table 1 (printed p. 159; PDF p. 11). https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-1446-5_8 ; author-hosted final chapter: https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/36052/36052.pdf


## 9. Current publication attribution and supporting clarification

The complete elementary theorem above remains accepted without mathematical repair. The current five-page note gives the same explicit constant and all-order construction, and separately proves the known coarse interval lower bound H_r>=1/[4(r+1)^2], extended fiberwise to a fixed product body in every dimension. This concerns the worst-case exponent, not every objective. The prior interval/Jacobi result is de Klerk-Laurent, Mathematics of Operations Research45(1)(2020),86-98, DOI10.1287/moor.2018.0983.

The quadratic proxy already appears in de Klerk-Laurent2018 (preprint Corollary4.3; final Corollary3) and Slot-Laurent. Endpoint localization and relative shell/core comparison have substantial classical precedents, including Totik-Varga2012, DOI10.1016/j.jmaa.2012.03.006, and Totik's2012 survey, DOI10.1090/conm/578/11471. Two independent audits and their reverse challenges verify a complete deduction assembled in2026 from Totik-Varga Theorem2.1, Markov core control, the relative homothety estimate and normalization. This is not evidence that an earlier paper printed the complete target theorem. No firstness, new mechanism, historical disclosure lineage or current worldwide openness is claimed.

Archive ROOT_PRIORITY_CLARIFICATIONS.md completes the standalone fallback's small orders, corrects the final proxy proof's PDF7/article6 locator, and distinguishes the false generic doubling shortcut from the independently proved special spectral geometry. Source bodies not read or redistributed remain explicitly identified. AI tools were used extensively; this is unrefereed, without external human peer review or formal proof-assistant certification.
edition_text.MOMENT_FORMULATION.md:
# Exact moment formulation at a non-simple boundary vertex

This example checks that the theorem applies beyond local affine cube/simplex models. It is not the proof of the general theorem, and a numerical SDP is not used as a certificate.

## Square pyramid and objective

Let

    K = {(x,y,z) : 0<=z<=1, -z<=x<=z, -z<=y<=z},
    f(x,y,z)=z.

K is a compact convex body in R^3. Its unique minimizer is the apex (0,0,0), incident to four facets, with four extreme rays in its tangent cone. A cube or simplex vertex in dimension three has three incident facets and three tangent-cone extreme rays. An invertible affine change preserves these incidences. Thus the apex is not locally affine-equivalent to any boundary point of a three-dimensional cube or simplex. In particular a local cube/simplex argument does not directly settle this vertex.

For integers a,b,c>=0, direct integration gives

    mu(a,b,c) = integral_K x^a y^b z^c dx dy dz
              = 0, if a or b is odd;
              = 4/((a+1)(b+1)(a+b+c+3)), otherwise.

Indeed, for even a,b the integrals over x and y are 2z^(a+1)/(a+1) and 2z^(b+1)/(b+1), after which the remaining z integral is elementary. In particular vol(K)=4/3.

## Full hierarchy: an exact generalized eigenvalue

Let I_r={alpha in N^3 : |alpha|<=r} and v_r=(x^alpha)_{alpha in I_r}. Define rational matrices

    H_r[alpha,beta] = mu(alpha_1+beta_1,alpha_2+beta_2,alpha_3+beta_3),
    Z_r[alpha,beta] = mu(alpha_1+beta_1,alpha_2+beta_2,alpha_3+beta_3+1).

H_r is positive definite: a nonzero real polynomial cannot vanish on the interior of K, so its squared integral over K is positive. For every nonzero coefficient vector c,

    integral_K z(c^T v_r)^2 / integral_K (c^T v_r)^2
       = (c^T Z_r c)/(c^T H_r c).

Any SOS q of degree<=2r is a sum of squares p_j^2 with each degree(p_j)<=r, because top-degree squares cannot cancel. Its objective divided by its normalization is a weighted average of these single-square Rayleigh quotients. Conversely every single square is feasible after normalization. Therefore

    f^(r) = lambda_min(Z_r,H_r),

exactly, with no numerical approximation. This is the general moment/eigenvalue formulation already described in the source literature, specialized here to fully explicit rational entries.

## A certified feasible witness

Since f=z itself is affine and nonnegative on K, it may be used directly in place of the quadratic proxy. For L=5 and m>=1 set

    Q_m(x,y,z)=A_m(z)^10,

with A_m defined in the proof. It is a single square, of degree 10m, feasible at hierarchy order r=5m after normalization. Its objective is exactly

    integral_0^1 z^3 A_m(z)^10 dz / integral_0^1 z^2 A_m(z)^10 dz.

The omitted factor 4 cancels. The sublevel-volume function is F(t)=(4/3)t^3 for 0<=t<=1, so the general dyadic estimate applies directly with dimension three. All mass in the whole pyramid is included. The finite rational checks accompanying this document confirm selected coefficient identities and exact witness integrals, but the all-order theorem is proved by the analytic argument, not by those finite tests.
edition_text.RESULT.md:
# Convex-body SOS-density convergence: result and scope

For every fixed compact convex body K in R^n with nonempty interior and every fixed real polynomial f, the normalized Lebesgue-measure hierarchy

    f^(r) = inf { integral_K f q dx : q is a global sum of squares,
                 degree(q)<=2r, integral_K q dx=1 }

satisfies

    0 <= f^(r)-min_K f <= C_{K,f}/r^2,     r>=1.

PROOF.md gives a complete explicit construction and constant. The witness is a single global square. The construction combines a quadratic Taylor upper estimator, homothetic growth of its sublevel volumes, and a fixed even power of a polynomial endpoint kernel. A dyadic shell estimate compares each tail directly with the same core mass that normalizes the density, avoiding a logarithmic loss.

MOMENT_FORMULATION.md gives an exact generalized-eigenvalue formulation at the nonsimple apex of a square pyramid. Its entries and feasible kernel witnesses use rational moments; no numerical SDP is treated as a certificate.

## Scope and source credit

The quadratic upper-estimator reduction is already present in Slot and Laurent's work, and polynomial concentration kernels are classical. The proof here is self-contained; no novelty or priority claim is made. The independent audit describes its bounded literature check and its limits.

The inspected Slot–Laurent paper's Theorem 11 gives O(log^2(r)/r^2) for general convex bodies with Lebesgue measure. Its concluding questions ask whether the logarithm can be removed. The final 2026 Laurent–Slot overview still lists that general rate in Table 1. These statements identify the source-matched improvement; they do not certify that the theorem was previously unknown. [Slot–Laurent paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.08142), [2026 overview](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/36052/36052.pdf).

The original Oberwolfach contribution has an incomplete displayed integral constraint. This result explicitly uses unit mass, consistent with the probability-density hierarchy in the full papers. It does not purport to solve an unnormalized formula. [Original report](https://ems.press/journals/owr/articles/16633).

## Limits

- The measure is Lebesgue. No claim is made for arbitrary unspecified reference measures.
- This is an upper O(r^-2) rate. It is not a two-sided Theta statement for each objective or for each body; constant objectives have zero error.
- The result is for the ordinary multivariate SOS-density hierarchy. It does not generally prove the same rate for densities restricted to s(f(x)), since the construction instead uses a quadratic upper proxy.
- The proof is an existence and rate argument; it does not assert an efficient way to find the minimizing point used to define the witness.
- Independent mathematical review is not a machine-checked formal proof, peer review, or a novelty certification.

The original problem identifier is OWR-16633-006 (corpus ID 30003990).


## Current acceptance and preprint scope

The full original normalized convex-body/Lebesgue target passes the root audit, fresh candidate-aware adversary, independently sealed question-only reconstruction, a fresh adversary of that reconstruction and the known lower example, and a materially distinct spectral derivation with its own fresh adversary. The spectral route imports the explicitly named standard Totik-Varga3.1 estimate; its empirical floating-point stress tests are not proof certificates.

The bounded historical and general-theory priority audits were sealed independently, then reverse-challenged. They establish substantial classical mechanism overlap and a complete consequence assembled from older endpoint-polynomial theory. They located no earlier explicit full-target theorem in inspected passages; this does not establish firstness or current openness. The known worst-case lower example is credited to de Klerk-Laurent2020. The current note, metadata and supporting records claim a complete proof of the historical target with that attribution, and no new-method or disclosure-lineage claim. See archive PRIORITY_ADJUDICATION.json under provenance and ROOT_PRIORITY_CLARIFICATIONS.md.

The preprint is titled "Quadratic convergence of SOS-density bounds on convex bodies" by Alec Kriebel, ORCID0009-0001-9320-500X. AI tools were used extensively in research, source checks, proofs, verification, writing and adversarial review. The note is unrefereed and has no external human peer review or formal machine-proof certification. Final package review and publication service receipts are maintained separately in the repository; this mathematical edition does not itself certify those operations.

metadata.title: Quadratic convergence of SOS-density bounds on convex bodies
metadata.description:
For every fixed compact convex body K in R^n with nonempty interior and every fixed real polynomial f, the normalized Lebesgue global sum-of-squares density hierarchy of degree at most 2r has error at most C(K,f)/r^2 for every integer r at least 1. A self-contained elementary proof gives an explicit constant and a single global square on the whole body. A quadratic Taylor upper proxy, homothetic sublevel growth, and a fixed power of an endpoint Dirichlet polynomial yield a normalized first-moment bound without a logarithmic loss. This proves the quadratic upper rate in the convex-body/Lebesgue regime of OWR-16633-006, with the probability-density unit-mass convention explicitly restored. The known interval linear example shows sharpness of the worst-case exponent; no positive matching lower rate for every objective is asserted.

The quadratic proxy, endpoint localization, and broad relative shell/core mass mechanism have substantial classical precedents, including de Klerk-Laurent, Slot-Laurent, and Totik-Varga. A deduction from older endpoint-polynomial theory was assembled during this audit; that does not show that an older source printed the complete target theorem. The bounded priority search located no earlier explicit full-target theorem in the inspected passages, and makes no claim of firstness, a new method, disclosure lineage, or current worldwide openness. Arbitrary reference measures, the restricted original-objective pushforward hierarchy for general nonconvex objectives, and an efficient method to find the minimizer are outside the result.

The deposit includes the note and a portable TeX-source, complete-proof, exact-arithmetic diagnostic, independent AI adversarial-review, integrity-verification, and bounded-priority archive. Numerical spectral stress tests are empirical, not proof certificates. Finite exact checks do not certify the infinite theorem. AI tools were used extensively in solving, derivations, source review, verification, drafting, and adversarial reviews. Unrefereed; no external human peer review, journal acceptance, or formal proof-assistant certification is claimed.
